parole.significato: A belief that spirits inhabit some or all classes of natural objects or phenomena.
parole.testo: From anima + -ism, from Latin anima (“life", "breath", "soul”). Dated sense from German Animismus, coined c. 1720 by physicist/chemist Georg Ernst Stahl (1660-1734) See anima mundi.

parole.significato: A dipeptide compound present in birds and other vertebrates, originally isolated from goose muscle.
parole.testo: From Latin anser (“goose”) + -ine, after German Anserin.

parole.significato: snow
parole.testo: From New Latin chion- (“snow”), chio, German chio, from Ancient Greek χιών (khiṓn, “snow”), χιόνι (khióni, “snow”), akin to Ancient Greek χειμών (kheimṓn, “winter”).

parole.significato: A repository for holding things; a hiding place or relicary.
parole.testo: From Latin conditorium, from condere (“to hide”). See recondite and reconditory. The cake shop is from German Konditorei

parole.significato: Instructive; that teaches.
parole.testo: From Latin docēns, present participle of doceō (“to teach”). In the meaning of a university grade, as used in some Central European countries, it is clipped version of private docent, privat-docent, from German Privatdozent, from German Dozent.

parole.significato: A disabling neurological disorder in which prolonged and repetitive contractions of muscles cause jerking, twisting mov…
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin dystonia, from German Dystonie. By surface analysis, dys- + -tonia.

parole.significato: In Semitic languages, the “adjective degree of superiority”. In some languages such as Arabic, the concepts of comparat…
parole.testo: From Latin ēlātus (“exalted, lofty, high”) + -ive. Possibly borrowed from German, which has produced a great deal of pioneering Semitist literature, and where Elativ is a common term for absolute superlative in all languages.

parole.significato: Moment of theoretical suspension of all action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin epocha or German Epoche, from Ancient Greek ἐποχή (epokhḗ). Doublet of epoch. This term was introduced by Husserl and other phenomenologists, although it also seems to be present in Aristotelian philosophy (as the concept did originate with Aristotle).

parole.significato: that which is; an entity, a being, an existent
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, coined by Ralph Manheim in his 1959 English translation of Martin Heidegger’s Einführung in die Metaphysik to render German Seiendes (as distinct from Sein) on the basis of *essens, a pseudo-Latin present participle of sum.

parole.significato: The unconscious impulsive component of the personality in the Freudian psychoanalytic model.
parole.testo: From New Latin id (“it”), chosen by Freud’s translator as a translation of his use of German Es (“it”) as a noun for this concept from the pronoun es (“it”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol In) with an atomic number of 49: a soft silvery-white metal.
parole.testo: Coined as a New Latin term from German Indigo (“indigo”), based on the color of its spectral lines.

parole.significato: An organ or other body part that is or can be turned inside out, especially an anterior portion of some annelid worms c…
parole.testo: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the theology of Martin Luther (1483–1546) or his followers, or the Lutheran church.
parole.testo: From the surname of German theologian and ecclesiastical reformer Martin Luther (1483–1546) + -an. Probably immediately from Renaissance Latin Lutheranus, or German Lutheraner. Luther is from an Old High German given name, from liut (“people”) + heri (“army”) (from Proto-Germanic *harjaz (“army; com

parole.significato: A bundle of neurons with their connective tissue sheaths, blood vessels and lymphatics.
parole.testo: Recorded since circa 1374 as Middle English nerve, from Medieval Latin nervus (“nerve”), from Latin nervus (“sinew”). Doublet of neuron and sinew. Verb sense 4 (“to get on (someone’s) nerves”) is chiefly a semantic loan from German nerven.

parole.significato: Synonym of zinc oxide, particularly white forms.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nihil album (“white nothing”), from late medieval confusion of German nichts (“nothing”) and nix with Latin nix (“snow, snow-white thing”), used for white forms of zinc oxide. Doublet of nill.

parole.significato: Synonym of zinc oxide, particularly white forms used in medicine and cosmetics.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nil and nihil (“nothing”) to represent German nichts and nix (“nothing”), confused with Latin nix (“snow, snow-white thing”), used for white forms of zinc oxide. Doublet of nihil album.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Paulownia, comprising deciduous flowering trees native to Asia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin paulownia, from German Pawlowna, transliterating Russian Па́вловна (Pávlovna), the patronymic of Anna Pavlovna.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pharaoh.
parole.testo: From Latin Pharaōn- (stem of Pharaō (“Pharaoh”)) + -ic, originally modelled on German pharaonisch.

parole.significato: That which is preferred.
parole.testo: From Latin praeferendum, modelled on German.

parole.significato: A female puer aeternus.
parole.testo: From Latin puella aeterna (“eternal girl”), female form of puer aeternus (“eternal boy”) (in Ovid, Metamorphoses), after use in German by CG Jung.

parole.significato: A child-god who is forever young.
parole.testo: From Latin puer aeternus (“eternal boy”) (in Ovid, Metamorphoses), after use in German by Carl Jung.

parole.significato: Various medieval and early modern coins or units of account
parole.testo: From Middle English solidus, from classical Latin solidus (“solid”), see below. Doublet of sol, sold, soldo, solid, sou, and xu. In numismatic and weight senses, via medieval Latin solidus (“various coins”), from Late Latin solidus (“a gold coin of the Roman Empire”). In chemical sense, via German S

parole.significato: Of, from, constituting, inhabiting, or pertaining to the Sudetes or the Sudetenland.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Sūdēticus, but with pronunciation influenced by German Sudeten and sudetisch.

parole.significato: According to the rules of an old drinking game in which the drinker upturned the empty cup and had to drink more if the…
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism from super- + naculum, nagulum, Latinized form of German Nagel, intended to mean “upon the nail”, after the German phrase auf den Nagel (trinken).

parole.significato: A muscle that tightens or stretches a part, or renders it tense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin tensor (“that which stretches”), equivalent to tense + -or. Anatomical sense from 1704. Introduced in the 1840s by William Rowan Hamilton as an algebraic quantity unrelated to the modern notion of tensor. The contemporary mathematical meaning was introduced (as German Tensor)

parole.significato: A person who sometimes wears clothes traditionally worn by and associated with the opposite sex; typically a male who c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trāns + vestītus, form of vestiō (“to clothe, to dress”) (as in English vestment, vest). Literally, a "cross-dresser". From transvestitism, from German Transvestitismus, coined in 1910 by Magnus Hirschfeld (the practice itself is much older).

parole.significato: Of or relating to tribes.
parole.testo: From Latin tribālis. By surface analysis, tribe + -al, first attested in the 1630s. parole.significato: relating to the square of a number
parole.testo: From New Latin zenzicus, zensicus, from zensus, Germanized from census / German zenzi (“square (of a number)”), from Italian censo (“property”), used in Medieval times to denote the algebraic square based on a translation of Arabic مَال (māl, “property, assets, estate; (obsolete) algebraic square”).
